The State Treasurer must publish a restricted-entity list by Oct 1, 2025 and update it at least semiannually. The bill becomes effective upon enactment. The State Treasurer must create and publish that list by October 1, 2025, and update it at least every six months. 109-1-LB663_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB663_Intro_Copy.docx LB663 amends county planning law (section 23-114.01). Key agency roles and changes:\n- Requires each county planning commission member and each county board member to complete two hours of role-specific education per term, developed and presented by the respective county attorney.\n- Requires county planning commissions and county boards to issue a statement of factual findings when granting or denying conditional-use/special-exception requests.\n- Establishes processing timelines: the commission has 30 days to assess completeness (10‑day notice for deficiencies), 30 days to reevaluate after additional information, and 90 days to decide or recommend; the board has analogous 30/10/30/90-day steps after receiving the commission’s recommendation.\n- Creates a presumption that applicants will comply with local, state, and federal requirements; challengers bear the burden of proof.\nAdministrative finance notes: members remain eligible for expense reimbursement, mileage per section 81-1176, and per diem up to $15/day not to exceed $1,000/year. No new appropriations specified. Adds a two-hour-per-term training requirement for each commission member and county board member on commissioner/board roles, with the training developed and presented by the respective county attorney. Establishes procedural rules for planning commissions and county boards: 30 days to declare an application complete (10‑day written notice if incomplete), 30 days after supplemental information to re-evaluate, and a 90‑day deadline to grant/deny or recommend action. Creates a presumption that applicants will comply with local, state, and federal requirements (burden on challengers to prove otherwise) and bars commissions/boards from conditioning a conditional use permit or special exception on obtaining other agency permits (though applicants still must secure required local, state, or federal permits). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB664_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB664_Intro_Copy.docx LB664 amends the Administrative Procedure Act (Reissue Revised Statutes §§84-906.02, 84-911). Agencies are required to permit any person to submit comments, written materials, or documentation for proposed or adopted rules or regulations, allow submissions electronically or by mail, and may not require in-person travel; agencies are also encouraged to solicit public comment via newspaper notice. The bill clarifies venue for declaratory-judgment challenges to rules: petitions may be filed in the district court of the county of the petitioner’s residence, the petitioner’s principal place of business, Lancaster County, or the county where the agency has its headquarters; the agency must be a party and may not restrict venue. Statutory procedures exclude Negotiated Rulemaking Act procedures. Original sections are repealed; the act takes effect immediately. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are provided. Adds requirements for state agencies and the district courts in administrative rule challenges: agencies must allow anyone to submit comments or supporting/opposing materials electronically or by mail and may not require in-person travel to submit them. 109-1-LB667_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB667_Final_Copy.docx LB667 amends §60-1438 of the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act to revise dealer compensation rules for diagnostic work and parts. Key agency-related provisions: dealers may establish an average parts markup by submitting sequential customer repair orders; manufacturers have 30 days to audit and 45 days after approval for the markup to take effect. A dealer may appeal a denial to the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Board, with the manufacturer bearing the burden to justify denial under the Act; an unreasonable denial is an Act violation subject to board enforcement. The bill defines compensation when a franchisor furnishes parts at no or reduced cost (uses "fair wholesale value") and preserves manufacturer/distributor audit and recall/warranty obligations. Claim/timing rules (six-month filing, 30-day approval/payment, audit periods) are clarified. Introduced in the Legislature and heard by the Transportation and Telecommunications Committee. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified. Adds rules under the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act governing dealer compensation and rate review. Key points:\n- Denials must be made pursuant to the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act.\n- When calculating part compensation, only retail sales not involving warranty repairs are used; markups for listed recommended maintenance items (oil, filters, fluids, brakes, spark plugs, wipers, tires, etc.) are excluded.\n- If a franchisor supplies a part free or at reduced cost for warranty work, the franchisor must pay the dealer the dealer's cost plus the dealer's markup, multiplied by the part's “fair wholesale value,” defined as the greatest of dealer paid amount, franchisor price-schedule cost, or cost of a substantially identical franchisor-listed part.\n- A manufacturer/distributor may request up to 100 additional dealer repair orders (from a selected 90-day window) to verify rates, may adjust payments, and dealers have 30 days to rebut; requests cannot be made more than once within 12 months.\nNo state agencies or departments (other than the cited Act) are named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. 109-1-LB686_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB686_Intro_Copy.docx LB686 prohibits Nebraska government entities and officials from knowingly keeping lists, records, or registries of privately owned firearms or firearm owners, except records maintained during criminal investigations, prosecutions, or as otherwise required by law. It also bars payment card networks and covered entities from requiring, incentivizing, or assigning merchant category codes that distinguish firearm retailers from other retailers, unless such coding is required by law. Enforcement is vested exclusively in the Nebraska Attorney General, who may investigate, issue notices to cease, seek injunctions, and request civil fines up to $1,000 per violation (with fines stayed pending appeal). No funding, appropriations, or budgetary changes are included. Adds prohibitions and an enforcement scheme enforced solely by the Attorney General. Key points:\n- Government entities may not maintain lists/registries of privately owned firearms or owners except records kept in the regular course of a criminal investigation or as otherwise required by law.\n- Payment card networks may not require or incentivize use of merchant category codes (MCCs) that distinguish firearm retailers; covered entities may not assign such distinguishing MCCs.\n- The Attorney General must investigate alleged violations (including by government entities), issue written notice, and if not remedied within 30 business days, sue for injunction. Courts must enjoin ongoing violations; continued noncompliance after 30 business days may produce civil fines up to $1,000 per violation (court to consider violator’s finances and constitutional harms). Fines are stayed on appeal. The AG has exclusive enforcement authority and the section’s remedies are exclusive. \n- No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are added. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB68_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB68_Intro_Copy.docx LB68 amends the Medical Assistance Act (adds section 3 and modifies §68-901) to require coverage and dispensing rules for self‑administered hormonal contraceptives. Private individual and group sickness and accident policies, hospital/medical/surgical expense policies, and self‑funded employee benefit plans (to the extent not preempted by federal law) must reimburse in‑network providers or dispensing entities per unit: initial prescriptions up to a three‑month supply and subsequent refills up to a twelve‑month supply regardless of enrollment at initial prescription. The bill prohibits requiring providers to prescribe 12‑month supplies and bars plans from imposing cost‑sharing for switching methods before exhausting a previously dispensed supply. Under the medical assistance program, the Department (administering Medicaid/family planning services) must ensure prescriptions permit one‑time dispensation of a 12‑month supply. No appropriations or budgetary allocations are included. Adds coverage requirements and a Medicaid directive. Insurers (individual/group sickness & accident, hospital/medical/surgical, and self‑funded employee plans where not federally preempted) must reimburse in‑network providers per unit for FDA‑approved self‑administered hormonal contraceptives: first prescription up to a three‑month supply; subsequent refills up to a twelve‑month supply even if the enrollee was not covered at the time of the first prescription. Clarifies providers are not required to prescribe 12‑month supplies and plans may not impose cost‑sharing for an alternative method if a person switches before using a dispensed supply. The state “department” administering the medical assistance (Medicaid) program must ensure a one‑time dispensation of a 12‑month supply for family planning. No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB690_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB690_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Transportation LB690 (as summarized) makes several changes affecting the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) and the Department of Transportation (DOT). If plate manufacturing costs exceed the statutory charge, funds otherwise credited to the DMV Cash Fund are first applied to the Highway Trust Fund to cover the excess. Separately, sales/use tax proceeds on aircraft (transactions on/after July 1, 2023) are credited to the DOT Aeronautics Capital Improvement Fund. Adds all‑terrain vehicles (ATVs) and utility‑type vehicles (UTVs) into the Motor Vehicle Registration Act when registered and operated under section 60‑6,356. Defines UTV (≤74" wide, ≤180" long, dry weight ≤2,000 lbs, four+ nonhighway tires) and excludes ATVs, golf cars, low‑speed vehicles. 109-1-LB692_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB692_Intro_Copy.docx Amends the School District Property Tax Limitation Act. The Department (responsible for calculation) must annually compute each district’s property tax request authority using a revised formula: prior-year property tax request (net of any prior-year excess) plus prior-year non-property-tax revenue minus investment income from special building funds, grown by the district’s base growth percentage, then reduced by current-year non-property-tax revenue and adjusted for documented errors. Nonproperty revenue categories lacking June 1 data default to prior-year amounts. The Department must certify the resulting authority to each school board. Changes to carryforward: districts may carry forward unused property tax request authority but must exclude increases attributable to base growth percentage under section 79-3405; the Department will calculate and report unused authority to school boards. Original sections 79-3403 and 79-3406 are repealed. No direct appropriations or new funding allocations are included. Adds language affecting school district property tax calculations: when computing the current amount, subtract any portion of last year’s property tax request that exceeded the district’s property tax request authority under section 79‑3405. Do not subtract increases to request authority that resulted from increases in the district’s base growth percentage under section 79‑3405. No specific state agencies or funding appropriations are created or changed. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB694_Intro General File Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB694_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Transportation The bill amends Section 39-210 (tourist-oriented directional sign panels) to require any applicant seeking qualification to provide the Department of Transportation assurance of compliance with applicable anti-discrimination laws, explicitly adding military or veteran status as a protected characteristic. 109-1-LB69_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB69_Final_Copy.docx LB69 amends statutes governing the Commission on African American Affairs. Key agency-related changes: the commission remains a 14-member body appointed by the Governor (members must be of African ancestry; initial appointments must include one immigrant/new American and one young professional); members are limited to two full four-year terms; commissioner names must be posted on the commission website; the commission elects its chair. 109-1-LB704_Final Passed Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB704_Final_Copy.docx LB704 amends Neb. Rev. Requires the department (child‑support agency) to initiate and complete a review when a noncustodial parent is incarcerated: parties must submit financial information (per §§43‑512.14 and 43‑512.17) within 30 days to the department and the facility administrator (per §47‑1003); the department must finish the review within 120 days and notify parties under §43‑512.13. If a decrease in support is denied, the department must schedule a conference for the incarcerated parent within 30 days (in person or virtual) and mail a notice to both parents specifying findings, format, date/time/location, evidence deadlines, waiver procedures, etc. The department must make a final determination within 30 days after the conference (or sooner if waived), decide whether to refer the order to the county or authorized attorney, and mail written notice. Notices to incarcerated parents go to the facility address and administrator. Final determinations are not contested cases under the Administrative Procedure Act. No funding or appropriation changes are included. DOCX | PDF
109-1-LB705_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB705_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Agriculture, Department of Economic Development, Department of Correctional Services, Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Revenue, Department of Transportation, Military Department The bill assigns the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to establish and maintain the medical‑cannabis patient/registered‑caregiver registry, issue/renew confidential registry cards, process applications, and promulgate rules. Department of Correctional Services employees are ineligible for licenses; DCS must provide drug‑treatment to sentenced persons and receives vehicle‑lettering exemptions (shared with DHHS, Agriculture, and the Military Department). Courts must notify the Department of Motor Vehicles of certain clean‑slate orders/juvenile abstracts. Effective July 1, 2023, aircraft sale/lease sales/use tax proceeds are credited to the Department of Transportation Aeronautics Capital Improvement Fund. - Department of Agriculture: Added duty to collaborate with the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission, Dept. of Revenue, and DHHS on regulation and oversight; no direct funding changes. \n- Department of Economic Development: Assigned administration of the new Medical Cannabis Business Equity Fund (may hold gifts, grants, legislative appropriations) and to run technical assistance, mentorship, and a grant program for social equity applicants and disproportionately impacted areas. 109-1-LB706_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB706_Intro_Copy.docx LB706 mandates law-enforcement dispatch screening for mental‑health indicators and requires calls identified as "Mental Health Priority" to notify and, when safe and practicable, be responded to by an APS social worker accompanying the officer; the APS social worker must lead de‑escalation and trauma‑informed interaction. The Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice (the commission) must set minimum policy standards, may provide a model policy, and will annually review agency compliance within its existing appropriations (including grants), reporting to the Governor and Legislature. Agencies with a pattern of noncompliance are ineligible for commission‑administered loans, grants, funds, or donations until corrected. Willful failure to comply can trigger discipline including revocation/suspension of officer certification. Financial enforcement: fines are collectible by the Attorney General and remitted to the State Treasurer. The bill also assigns related duties to the Department of Health and Human Services concerning APS social workers. Requires law enforcement agencies to have dispatch personnel screen calls with a checklist for mental‑health indicators, flag qualifying calls as a "Mental Health Priority," notify the nearest unit and an APS social worker, and share mental‑health information with responders. When safe/practicable, officers responding to such calls must be accompanied by an APS social worker, who will lead the interaction using de‑escalation and trauma‑informed care. Agencies must adopt written dispatch/APS‑accompaniment policies and submit them to the commission, which will set minimum standards and may distribute a model policy (not mandatory except for delinquent agencies). The commission will annually review compliance and report to the Governor and Legislature, using only existing appropriations (including any awarded grants). Agencies with patterns of noncompliance are ineligible for commission‑administered loans, grants, funds, or donations until cured. DOCX | PDF

109-1-LB99_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 1 (2025) 109 1 LB99_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services This bill amends definitions and directs duties for the Department of Correctional Services. It codifies “Department” and “Director of Correctional Services,” treats committed offenders and facilities as those under the department, and defines “restrictive housing.” It requires the department to limit use of restrictive housing (no more than 15 consecutive days; single-occupancy cells unless inmates consent), to adopt Administrative Procedure Act rules establishing restrictive-housing levels, placement criteria, and individualized transition plans developed with the committed offender. The department must promulgate rules addressing risks for vulnerable populations (bar placement in restrictive housing except for immediate segregation pending classification) and may develop secure mental-health housing that ensures meaningful access to social interaction, exercise, stimulation, and therapeutic programming. Prohibits an electric supplier from retiring, shutting down, ceasing operation of, or substantially altering any electric generation facility — including privately developed renewable facilities — if the supplier has customers waiting for service, except where: (a) the action is required by federal or state law; (b) the facility is mechanically unsafe; (c) the facility is irreparably damaged by a natural disaster; or (d) continued operation is uneconomical. Requires the electric supplier’s governing body to adopt a resolution identifying the reasons for the proposed action and to cite at least one of the four exceptions. No specific government agencies or departments are named beyond references to “federal or state law,” and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1027_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1027_Intro_Copy.docx LB1027 amends Chapter 70 (article 10) to tighten oversight of privately developed renewable generation. 109-2-LB1028_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1028_Intro_Copy.docx LB1028 amends the Livestock Waste Management Act to require each large concentrated animal feeding operation (as defined by 40 C.F.R. 122.23, effective January 1, 2026) to register and annually update its nutrient management plan with "the department" and publish the plan and supporting documentation on the department's website. 109-2-LB1035_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1035_Intro_Copy.docx LB1035 amends the Property and Casualty Insurance Rate and Form Act and changes duties and limits tied to the Director of Insurance (the "director"). 109-2-LB1036_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1036_Intro_Copy.docx LB1036 amends Neb. Evid. Rule 27-404. It expressly permits admission of extrinsic evidence that is "inextricably intertwined" with the charged crime and clarifies when evidence of other crimes, wrongs, or acts may be used for non‑character purposes (motive, intent, identity, etc.). Procedural requirements: the prosecution must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the accused committed the other act and, when relying on the inextricably‑intertwined basis, that the evidence meets that standard; the proof must be made outside the jury's presence; and, upon request, the court must give a limiting jury instruction. A repeal of the original section is included. Agencies affected: Nebraska courts and prosecuting attorneys. No changes to funding or appropriations. Adds a definition and procedural rules for "other crimes, wrongs, or acts" being "inextricably intertwined" with the charged offense: such evidence is inextricably intertwined if it (1) forms part of the factual setting, (2) is so blended/connected that proving the charged crime requires proving the other acts, or (3) is necessary to present a coherent picture of the charged crime. It also provides that, when offered under the specified subdivision, the court must (implicitly) address that intertwining and, upon the defendant’s request, must instruct the jury to consider the evidence only for the limited purpose for which it was admitted. No government agencies or departments are mentioned and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1037_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1037_Intro_Copy.docx LB1037 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §§77-2602.05, 77-2602.06, and 77-2603.01. The bill limits grounds for declining or delaying talks (e.g., tribal regulation of cannabis) and prescribes required agreement elements (duration, administration, enforcement, waiver of sovereign immunity, division of proceeds, dispute resolution, reporting/auditing). It preserves the Tax Commissioner’s refund process and allows negotiated refund formulas (capped at taxes paid by tribal entities). Section 77-2603.01 expressly permits tribal cigarette stamps under such agreements. No direct appropriations or budget allocations are included. Requires the Governor (or a designated representative) to enter into good‑faith negotiations with any federally recognized Nebraska tribe that submits a written request. Negotiations must begin within 60 days, include at least one session every 90 days while active, and continue until an agreement or a joint written impasse. The Governor may choose whether to execute an agreement but may not refuse, terminate, or unreasonably delay negotiations based primarily on a tribe's lawful exercise of authority on matters unrelated to cigarette/tobacco taxation (e.g., tribal cannabis regulation). The negotiation scope explicitly covers collection, allocation, and refunds of cigarette and other tobacco taxes and amounts held or paid into escrow under section 69‑2703 and related Master Settlement Agreement statutes. 109-2-LB1041_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1041_Intro_Copy.docx LB1041 requires Nebraska cities, villages, and counties to allow at least one accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on the same lot as a single‑family residence, subject to building codes and size limits (≤1,000 sq ft or 50% of the primary residence, as specified). Local historic ordinances, deed or association restrictions, and Condominium Act limits may still prohibit or limit ADUs. Manufactured/mobile homes used as ADUs must be placed on permanent foundations and assessed as real property. The bill bars cities/counties from imposing requirements on ADU placement, appearance, parking, utility connections, impact fees, occupancy (owner‑occupancy, familial/employment, income/age restrictions), or landlord‑tenant rules more restrictive than those for single‑family homes or the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Permits meeting statutory requirements must be approved on the same timeline as single‑family permits; conflicting local ordinances/resolutions are void. No changes to state appropriations or agency funding are included. Adds requirements for local governments: cities (including villages) and counties must allow at least one accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on a single‑family lot, subject to building codes, size limits (≤1,000 sq ft or ≤50% of the primary dwelling), and narrow exceptions (historic, deed/HOA/condominium restrictions). Manufactured/mobile ADUs must be placed on permanent foundations and assessed as real property for tax purposes. Cities and counties are prohibited from imposing more restrictive placement, appearance, rental, parking, occupancy, utility, impact‑fee, or street/sidewalk requirements than those for the primary residence. 109-2-LB1045_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1045_Intro_Copy.docx Creates the Nebraska Public Housing Preservation Trust, a new public trust that will contract with local housing agencies (agreements required by Jan 1, 2027) to preserve and rehabilitate public housing while retaining public ownership. 109-2-LB1050_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1050_Intro_Copy.docx LB1050 amends the Nebraska Reading Improvement Act, assigning duties primarily to the State Department of Education and to local school boards/districts. The department must approve and publish approved reading assessments and threshold performance levels (including statewide and alternate grade‑3 thresholds by Oct 1, 2026), create a test‑based student portfolio option by Jan 1, 2027, develop a professional learning system for evidence‑based K–3 and early childhood reading instruction, provide technical assistance, coordinate regional coaches with educational service units, adopt rules, and file an annual report (by Sept. 30) with the Clerk of the Legislature. School boards must administer assessments, provide supplemental reading intervention programs and individualized plans, and (beginning 2027‑28) retain third‑grade students with persistent reading deficiencies from advancing to grade four (with exceptions). Intent to appropriate $2 million annually from the Education Future Fund for FY2024‑25 through FY2026‑27 to the Department for regional coaches/training. - The state Department of Education (referred to as "the department") must by Oct 1, 2026 set and publish threshold performance levels for the statewide grade‑3 reading assessment and for alternate grade‑3 reading assessments. \n- By Jan 1, 2027 the department must create and publish a test‑based student portfolio option, including criteria and a threshold level, to demonstrate grade‑3 reading mastery. \n- Students not meeting those thresholds are designated as having a persistent reading deficiency and, beginning in 2027–28, school boards must retain such students in grade three (with specified exemptions for assessment‑exempt students, certain special‑education/504/ADA students after two years of intervention and prior retention, and students with two years of intervention and prior cumulative retention). No student may be retained under this rule more than once. \n- Schools must notify parents by Feb 1 if a third‑grader remains deficient as of Jan 1 and offer meetings to revise individualized reading plans. \n- Required supports include home reading strategies, a transitional instructional setting option, and before/after‑school intervention by teachers/tutors trained in reading intervention. \n- Federal statutes referenced: Section 504 (Rehabilitation Act) and Title II (ADA). \n- No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. 109-2-LB1056_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1056_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Labor LB1056 references the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics as the source for Consumer Price Index data used in benefit adjustments. The bill ties the annual cost‑of‑living adjustment (COLA) for weekly workers’ compensation income benefits (beginning 2027) to the 12‑month percent change in the CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI‑W) as prepared by the U.S. Department of Labor, BLS (with a 1% floor). It also ties the annual burial expense cap adjustment (beginning 2023) to the 12‑month percent change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI‑U) as prepared by the U.S. Department of Labor, BLS (with a 1% floor and 2.75% annual cap). The bill contains no changes to Department of Labor funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. No new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department of Labor are included.\n\nSubstantive additions that may affect Dept. of Labor operations:\n- Employers must pay reasonable costs for interpreter services (medical, surgical, hospital, employer- or examiner‑required exams, and independent medical exams); interpreters chosen from the Nebraska Supreme Court register (Rule 6‑702). Employers must provide notices in a language the employee understands.\n- Beginning Jan 1, 2027, weekly workers’ compensation benefits lasting >12 months receive annual COLA adjustments: COLA = greater of 1% or the 12‑month CPI‑W change (BLS). The Nebraska Workers’ Compensation Court sets the annual COLA; adjustments are computed to the next whole dollar and capped by statutory maximums.\n- Maximum weekly benefit increases to 200% of the state average weekly wage (computed per section 48‑121.02) starting Jan 1, 2027, subject to possible annual suspension by the Governor after a public hearing.\n\nPotential Dept. of Labor impacts: annual provision of the state average weekly wage figure and coordination on wage/CPI data used to compute caps and COLAs. 109-2-LB1062_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1062_Intro_Copy.docx LB1062 primarily affects actions by the Director of Insurance (and related state insurance regulators) and the State Treasurer:\n\n- Director of Insurance: expanded authority to impose retaliatory measures under reciprocal statutes; verify nonresident producer licensure via the NAIC producer database (or successor) or by contacting the home-state regulator; automatically cancel nonresident licenses if home-state licensure is inactive; issue orders, hold hearings under the Administrative Procedure Act, and levy administrative fines (up to $1,000 per violation) for producer licensing violations.\n- Pharmacy Benefit Manager (PBM) regulation (Director): authorizes rules, requires PBM licensure, sets a nonrefundable application fee cap of $500 and an annual renewal fee cap of $250, imposes $100/day fines for late PBM renewals and permits suspension until compliance, and requires PBMs to notify the director of material ownership/control changes.\n- State Treasurer: receives PBM fines for constitutionally prescribed distribution. Adds authority for the director (insured-regulatory director) to cancel a nonresident license when the licensee's home-state license is inactive (suspension, revocation, lapse, surrender, etc.). The licensee may demand a hearing within 30 days; the hearing must be held within 30 days under the Administrative Procedure Act. If the director has notice a nonresident failed to keep a resident license in good standing, the nonresident license is automatically revoked. For pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs): failure to comply with renewal/related requirements triggers a $100/day fine while transacting business and suspension if renewal/fee not received by the license anniversary. The director remits fines to the State Treasurer for distribution per Article VII, §5 of the Nebraska Constitution. The director may grant one 30‑day extension without fine/suspension; PBMs must immediately notify the director of material ownership/control changes. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1063_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1063_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Banking and Finance Defines "Department" as the Department of Banking and Finance and "Director" as the Director of Banking and Finance. The Director is directed to (1) presume lack of such proof indicates unfitness for licensure or control acquisitions, (2) within 30 days issue forms/instructions and an order requiring information showing applicants are not foreign adversary persons, and (3) within 60 days request supplemental information from existing licensees/applicants and initiate revocation proceedings under section 8-2734 for noncompliance or reasonable suspicion. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are provided. Creates new foreign-adversary screening and reporting duties for the Department of Banking and Finance (the director under the Nebraska Money Transmitters Act). Key points:\n- Defines “foreign adversary person” and requires applicants, licensees, key individuals, and persons in control to certify they are not such persons and provide verifiable supporting information.\n- Director may presume lack of character/fitness and deny, block acquisition, or revoke licenses if certification/verification is not established.\n- On enactment the rules apply to all existing and future licenses; within 60 days the director must request supplemental information from licensees/applicants and may initiate revocation proceedings for noncompliance; within 30 days the director must issue forms/instructions and an order imposing the new information requirements.\n- No appropriations, funding, or budget allocations are added or changed. 109-2-LB1065_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1065_Intro_Copy.docx This bill revises procedures and responsibilities for updating and distributing the Constitution of Nebraska. Agencies and duties:\n\n- Revisor of Statutes: must compile an updated constitution after each statewide election adopting a constitutional amendment (including source notes and notes identifying sections declared unconstitutional). May compile updates to notes after other statewide general elections and must notify the Secretary of State and Clerk of the Legislature if doing so.\n- Attorney General: must promptly notify the Revisor when a section is declared unconstitutional or inoperative.\n- Board of State Canvassers: completion of the canvass triggers a 10-calendar-day deadline for transmission.\n- Secretary of State: reviews the Revisor’s draft, determines accuracy, certifies the copy, and maintains every certified edition.\n- Clerk of the Legislature: posts the certified copy online, includes it in session laws, prints pamphlets on request; certified copies are official prima facie evidence.\n\nNo funding, appropriations, or budget changes are included. The act takes effect immediately under an emergency clause. Adds a procedural deadline and duties for three state entities: after the board of state canvassers completes its canvass of a statewide election that adopts a constitutional amendment, the Revisor of Statutes must, within ten calendar days, promptly prepare and transmit the updated statutory copy to the Secretary of State for review and certification under subsection (2). 109-2-LB1066_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1066_Intro_Copy.docx LB1066 requires each newly sworn Nebraska legislator to complete a "civics assessment" within 90 days. The term is defined as the civics portion of the U.S. Naturalization Test administered by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (Department of Homeland Security) or an equivalent exam designated by the Secretary of State or the State Department of Education. The Clerk of the Legislature must administer a 20-question randomly selected assessment, certify each member's raw score to that member, and publish raw scores on the Legislature's official website and in members' official biographies; individual question responses remain confidential. Completion is mandatory but passage is not and does not affect constitutional qualifications or officeholding. Members who do not pass are invited (but not required) to voluntary seminars offered by the Nebraska State Historical Society or the Legislative Research Office. No funding or appropriations are specified. Adds a requirement that each legislator complete a 20-question civics assessment within 90 days of taking office. Agencies and roles named:\n- United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (Department of Homeland Security): source of the civics portion of the U.S. Naturalization Test; Secretary of State or the State Department of Education may designate an equivalent test.\n- Clerk of the Legislature: administers the exam, selects questions, calculates and certifies raw scores to members, keeps individual answers confidential, and publishes raw scores on the Legislature’s website and in members’ official biographies.\n- Nebraska State Historical Society and Legislative Research Office: may offer voluntary civic literacy seminars for members who do not achieve a passing score.\n\nNo changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. 109-2-LB1075_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1075_Intro_Copy.docx LB1075 revises Nebraska election and village-governance statutes, reallocating duties among the Secretary of State, election commissioners, county clerks, county canvassing boards and treasurers, county central committees, courts, the State Records Administrator, and the Nebraska State Historical Society. Key administrative changes: Secretary of State must prepare/preserve county vote abstracts, provide abstracts to state party chairs on request, post vote‑count device test certifications, prescribe election‑worker training, and accept party filings 60 days before primaries allowing unaffiliated participation. County officials’ duties are expanded/clarified for precinct creation/size, notices/sample ballots, mail/replacement ballots, signature/ID verification timelines, provisional‑ballot verification (within seven business days), canvass records, and timely abstract delivery (counties may retrieve abstracts by messenger at official expense; negligent officials are liable). Village boards may authorize clerks to issue warrants during majority vacancies, subject to later board review. Fiscal changes: a temporary $100 per‑precinct recount fee (through 12/31/2026) payable to county treasurers and deposited to county general funds (refundable if result is overturned), revised cost‑allocation rules (cost‑per‑precinct, $100 minimum, alternate billing for some public power and school elections), and political subdivisions bear costs of canceled special elections. No statewide appropriations are made. Adds procedural and limited fiscal provisions affecting local and state election officials and village governments. Key agencies: village board of trustees and village clerk (clerk may prepare claims/issue warrants only when >50% of trustees’ seats are vacant and only for board‑approved or legally/contractually required expenditures; board must annually authorize this and later review claims). Election agencies: Secretary of State, election commissioners, and county clerks (may accept cancellations of special elections through the fourth Thursday before the election; Secretary must notify commissioners/clerks when a party permits unaffiliated voters in its primary). Fiscal changes: the political subdivision that cancels a special election pays related costs (per §32‑1202); counties must bear overnight delivery costs for vote abstracts; recount fees set at $100 per precinct through Dec. 31, 2026, with candidates liable for any excess actual costs. Also limits who may copy precinct sign‑in registers and criminalizes ballot forgery. DOCX | PDF

109-2-LB1079_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1079_Intro_Copy.docx LB1079 amends §29-2221 (habitual criminal enhancements). It prescribes mandatory minimum and maximum imprisonment terms to be served in Department of Correctional Services adult correctional facilities: generally a 10‑year minimum and up to 60 years; a 25‑year minimum (up to 60) for specified serious offenses or defined combinations of prior felonies; a 3‑year minimum (up to 20) where the current and prior felonies are violations of subsection (3) of §28‑416; and a 3‑year minimum (up to 20) for violations of §§28‑509–28‑518 when two or more prior felonies are similar. The bill maintains court procedures requiring the indictment/information to allege habitual status (not disclosed to juries) and a separate court hearing before sentencing. The original §29‑2221 is repealed. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds a sentencing enhancement: when a felony violates sections 28-509 to 28-518 and the defendant has two or more prior felony convictions for those same or substantially similar offenses (including convictions from other states or federal law), the mandatory minimum sentence is three years and the maximum is twenty years. The enhancement applies even if one or more prior convictions did not include a term of imprisonment. No government agencies, departments, or funding/appropriation changes are mentioned. DOCX | PDF

109-2-LB1097_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1097_Intro_Copy.docx Creates the State and Political Subdivisions Sexual Abuse Liability Act, making the State of Nebraska, state agencies, and political subdivisions liable for child sexual abuse and abuse of individuals with developmental disabilities similarly to private actors. The Act waives sovereign immunity for these claims and exempts them from the State Tort Claims Act and Political Subdivisions Tort Claims Act (and their limits on damages, jury availability, notice requirements, and statutes of limitations). No funding or appropriation changes are included. Creates the "State and Political Subdivisions Sexual Abuse Liability Act," making the state, state agencies, and political subdivisions liable like private parties for tort claims arising from child sexual abuse and abuse of individuals with developmental disabilities. Definitions of "state agency," "political subdivision," and "employee" are tied to existing statutes (sections 81-8,210, 13-903, 71-1107). The act waives sovereign immunity for these entities, removes applicability of the State Tort Claims Act and Political Subdivisions Tort Claims Act (including their limits, notice rules, jury/damage limits, and statutes of limitation), and bars writs of execution against the state, state agencies, or political subdivisions for claims under this act. 109-2-LB1104_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1104_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Revenue LB1104 authorizes the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) and the Department of Revenue (DOR) to determine that a vehicle or trailer kept in Nebraska more than 30 days has situs here and that a resident owner is avoiding required taxes/fees. Specified factors (e.g., Nebraska initial purchaser, operation/storage in-state, insurance coverage, resident affiliation with nominal owner) support a rebuttable presumption that the resident must register the vehicle and pay motor vehicle taxes/fees and sales/use tax. DMV or DOR must notify the presumed owner, who has 30 days to pay or appeal (DMV appeals to the Director with a hearing officer under the Administrative Procedure Act; DOR appeals under §77‑2709). Unpaid amounts incur a 50% late fee remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Highway Trust Fund; other penalties in §§60‑3,164 and 60‑3,170 apply. Creates authority for the Department of Motor Vehicles or Department of Revenue to deem a vehicle or trailer kept >30 days in Nebraska and establish situs based on specified ties to a Nebraska resident. Such a determination creates a rebuttable presumption that the resident is the owner, must register the vehicle in Nebraska, and owes motor vehicle taxes, fees, and sales/use tax. The agency making the determination must notify the resident, who has 30 days to pay or appeal. DMV appeals go to the Director of Motor Vehicles (hearing officer; APA procedures); Revenue appeals follow section 77-2709. Unpaid amounts incur a 50% late fee remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Highway Trust Fund. No other appropriations or budget changes. DOCX | PDF

109-2-LB1107_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1107_Intro_Copy.docx LB1107 amends the Rural Road Improvement District Act, authorizing county-level procedures and finance mechanisms. Key actors: county boards, county clerks, county governments, county engineers, special counsel, and local advisory committees; counties may also contract with state or federal agencies. Financial changes: counties may use progress warrants and issue general-obligation bonds (≤20-year maturity) to fund improvements; bond repayment relies on a sinking fund of special assessments and contributions and, if needed, an annual countywide tax to cover deficiencies. Counties may create per-district or a single county rural road improvement fund; advisory-committee expenses are reimbursable and charged to project cost. Special assessments become liens, may be paid in up to ten annual installments with interest (rate capped by section 45-104.01 or as set by the board prior to due date), and delinquent installments bear statutory interest. Completion transfers roads to county maintenance; districts may impose a special maintenance levy up to $0.035 per $100. The bill repeals several existing sections. Adds procedures for forming rural road improvement districts, emphasizing county-level actors: the county board (which cannot adopt a resolution in the same meeting it is proposed) and the county clerk (who receives written owner objections and petitions). Property owners owning >50% of area can block a hearing by filing objections. The board may create either a separate fund per district or a single county "rural road improvement fund." That fund is credited with money, special assessments, bond proceeds, special levies and related receipts. Counties may accept grants, contract for and purchase improvements, and issue bonds under §39‑1648 to pay costs (bonds mature 20 years). Unpaid special assessments accrue interest after the due date. Petitions for boundary changes, withdrawals, consolidations, or dissolution are filed with the county clerk. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1108_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1108_Intro_Copy.docx LB1108 amends procurement rules in Neb. statutes governing joint entities (electric-generation joint authorities) and districts (public power districts) by establishing tiered sealed-bid thresholds: $750,000 for entities/districts with gross revenue under $500 million and $1,500,000 for those with gross revenue of $500 million or more. Above those thresholds contracts require advertised sealed bids (advertised once in local general-circulation newspapers). The bill preserves and clarifies exceptions—contracts involving radioactive material, technologically complex or unique equipment, procurements from electric utilities or alliances, maintenance/repairs, original-manufacturer replacement parts, used equipment purchases, and emergency work—subject to engineer certification, two-thirds governing-body approval where required, and specified public notice. Sections 13-824.01, 13-824.02, and 70-637 are amended; original versions are repealed. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds fee/threshold language applying $750,000 for joint entities with gross revenue under $500 million and $1,500,000 for those with gross revenue of $500 million or more. It also authorizes the governing body of a joint entity, upon sudden or unexpected damage or a regulatory body order preventing compliance with sections 13-824.01–13-824.03, to declare an emergency and proceed with necessary work on electric generating facilities without first complying with those sections. 109-2-LB1111_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1111_Intro_Copy.docx LB1111 amends electric utility law to add reporting and regulatory duties centered on the Nebraska Power Review Board and public power suppliers. The bill requires the representative organization to file an annual data center load report with the Nebraska Power Review Board. It defines "data center," "large data center" (peak demand ≥20 MW), and "public power supplier" (public power districts, municipal electric utilities, or other government electric providers). Public power suppliers must: ensure large data centers pay full costs for new service and infrastructure upgrades, avoid cost-shifting to other retail customers, require decommissioning plans and security, conduct load studies before imposing requirements, and publish specified project details on their websites. Public power suppliers may impose cost-recovery measures (e.g., letters of credit) on cryptocurrency mining operations and may interrupt service under established policies. No appropriations or budgetary changes are included. Adds an annual data‑center load report requirement: a representative organization must file detailed data (name, owners, size, address, electricity demand and suppliers, contracts, T&D upgrades, efficiency/renewables commitments, service life, etc.) with the board.\n\nAssigns duties and rate‑setting constraints to public power suppliers: ensure large data centers (≥20 MW peak) pay full costs for new electric service and infrastructure upgrades, cannot shift costs or stranded‑asset risk to other retail customers, and must bear decommissioning costs. Public suppliers must require centers to post a decommissioning bond within one year of commercial operation, submit decommissioning plans, provide county/municipal permits, enter community benefit agreements, and propose private/self‑generation options. Public suppliers must limit service if private/self‑supply is available and interconnect such sources.\n\nNo explicit changes to agency funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. DOCX | PDF

The bill amends the definition of supplier to exclude microbreweries and harmonizes cross-references. The Nebraska Liquor Control Commission retains roles: approving extensions of temporary wholesaler appointments, receiving notices of temporary service interruptions, and receiving supplier notices for test marketing. Legal remedies remain through Nebraska state or federal courts. No funding, appropriations, or budgetary changes are included. Operative date: October 1, 2026. Adds an exemption to statutes 53-201 through 53-223 for agreements entered into, amended, or renewed on or after the act’s operative date between a microbrewery (per §53-103.21) and a wholesaler. Any continuous or indefinite agreement existing before the operative date is deemed terminated on October 1, 2027 unless the parties execute a new written agreement beforehand; such new agreements are covered by the exemption. The term “supplier” is clarified to exclude microbreweries. No government agencies, departments, appropriations, or funding changes are referenced. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1116_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1116_Intro_Copy.docx LB1116 amends the Sports Arena Facility Financing Assistance Act and affects the following state entities and funds:\n\n- State Treasurer: transfers certified amounts to a newly created Sports Arena Facility Support Fund. \n- State Investment Officer: invests fund assets under the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. \n- Legislature: appropriates distributions from the Support Fund to approved political subdivisions per statutory formulas (generally up to 70% of specified state sales tax revenues for most facilities; 25% for sports complexes in cities of the second class or villages). Excess after year ten may revert to the General Fund. \n- Fund and grant limits: overall cap of $100 million per facility; large public stadiums limited to $25 million total and $1.25 million annually (no payments before July 1, 2027), though approvals on/after July 19, 2024 may fund up to 100% of final cost within those caps. \n- Residual tax allocations: portions directed to the Support the Arts Cash Fund, Convention Center Support Fund, or Civic and Community Center Financing Fund as specified. \n- Board procedures: public hearing within 30 days of application review and board decision within 30 days after hearing; temporary approvals become permanent upon voter approval or issuance of building permit. \n- Effective immediately due to emergency clause. Adds deadlines for "the board" to decide on applications: the board must determine approval within 30 days after completing its review (or, for applications filed on/after the act's effective date, within 30 days after the public hearing required by section 13‑3105). For applications filed before the effective date, the decision deadline is 30 days after that public hearing or 30 days after the effective date, whichever is later. Applications are deemed approved unless the board finds the project ineligible or that state assistance would not be in the state's best interest. No specific state agency beyond "the board" or any changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are mentioned. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1117_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1117_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Revenue The bill requires qualifying children applying for First Responder tuition waivers to file with the Department of Revenue documentation each year proving that the first responder or eligible disabled person (through whom the child claims the waiver) was employed as a first responder/eligible disabled person and resided in Nebraska. If a first responder dies in the line of duty after the child's application, the child must instead file with the Department of Revenue proof that, at the time of death, the first responder was employed as a first responder and resided in Nebraska.\n\nSeparately, the bill (effective July 1, 2028) directs the Coordinating Commission for Postsecondary Education, subject to available appropriations, to reimburse institutions for 50% of tuition waivers (procedures and prorating rules apply). No provisions directly affect the Department of Revenue. The added text creates a funding mechanism (effective July 1, 2028, subject to available appropriations) requiring the Coordinating Commission for Postsecondary Education to reimburse the University of Nebraska, state colleges, and community colleges for 50% of tuition waivers provided under section 80-411 (linked to the First Responder Recruitment and Retention Act). Institutions must submit documentation in a commission-prescribed form. If state appropriations are insufficient, reimbursements will be prorated across institutions to match the appropriation; prorated claims may not be refiled. No specific appropriation amount or new revenue source is designated. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1118_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1118_Intro_Copy.docx LB1118 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §87-302 (Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act) to classify specified conduct by social media platforms that accept payment for advertising as deceptive trade practices. It requires such platforms to implement: advertiser identity verification; unlawful-impersonation detection/mitigation; automated and manual fraud-detection systems; measures to prevent repeat offending advertisers; a clear user reporting tool for suspected fraud; and a process for law enforcement to report suspected fraudulent ads. After a user or law-enforcement report, platforms must investigate and determine within seven days whether an advertisement is fraudulent. No state agency funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified. The bill repeals the original section. Adds requirements for paid-ad social media platforms to implement advertiser identity verification; unlawful-impersonation detection/mitigation; automated and manual fraud detection; measures to prevent repeat offending advertisers; a conspicuous user fraud-reporting tool; and a process allowing law enforcement to report suspected fraudulent ads. After a report by a user or law enforcement, platforms must investigate within seven days and determine whether the ad is fraudulent (and, if so, take further action—text cuts off). No specific government agencies or departments are named beyond generic "law enforcement," and there are no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations included. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1119_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1119_Intro_Copy.docx LB1119 amends Nebraska’s Age-Appropriate Online Design Code Act. It cites federal agencies and statutes: the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) — delegating determination of “dark patterns” to the FTC and referencing FTC rules implementing the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) for the definition of “parent” — and the Federal Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) for periodic adjustment of the revenue threshold using the Consumer Price Index. The bill tightens obligations on covered online services (data minimization, retention limits, prohibitions on targeted ads to minors, notification/time restrictions, deletion/unpublishing within 15 days) and repeals prior sections. No changes to state funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Adds a list of specific design features (e.g., infinite scroll, autoplay, visible engagement counts, gamification like streaks/badges, clustered notifications, virtual currencies/digital purchases, image‑altering filters, repeated account‑creation prompts, ephemerality, barriers to deleting accounts, and features that mimic human intimacy) that can trigger coverage. Requires covered online services to prohibit a single setting that simultaneously makes all default privacy protections less protective for covered minors and to avoid prompting minors to weaken privacy unless strictly necessary to access a requested feature. Requires a prominent tool for covered minors to request account unpublishing/deletion and mandates honoring such requests within 15 days. No government agencies or departments are mentioned, and no funding or appropriation changes are included. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1120_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1120_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Revenue The bill requires licensees under both the Nebraska Lottery and Raffle Act and the Nebraska Small Lottery and Raffle Act to register each progressive‑jackpot, multi‑draw lottery/raffle (e.g., Queen of Hearts) with the Department of Revenue and to post the game rules at the sale/conduct location. It authorizes sales via vending/dispensing devices and grants the Department of Revenue rule‑making authority to regulate such games. The bill’s preamble states it provides powers and duties to the Department of Revenue. It also reduces the required prize‑payout floor for lotteries/raffles conducted under the new progressive‑jackpot section from 65% to 50% of gross proceeds. No direct appropriations or other budget allocations to the department are specified. - Authorizes licensed organizations and qualifying nonprofits to run progressive‑jackpot, multi‑draw lotteries/raffles (e.g., “Queen of Hearts”).\n- Requires each such game to be registered with the Department of Revenue and game rules to be posted where the game is run or tickets are sold.\n- Allows ticket sales through vending/dispensing devices.\n- Grants the Department of Revenue authority to adopt and promulgate rules and regulations governing these games.\n- Notes a provision that a lottery/raffle under section 4 need only allocate 50% of gross proceeds to prizes.\n\nNo provisions in the added text change Department of Revenue funding, appropriations, or departmental budget allocations. 109-2-LB1121_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1121_Intro_Copy.docx Creates the Recreational Vehicle Industry Regulation Act and moves regulation of recreational vehicles out of the Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act. Expands the Nebraska Motor Vehicle Industry Licensing Board (chaired by the Director of Motor Vehicles) to include two new gubernatorial appointees—a licensed recreational vehicle dealer and a licensed recreational vehicle manufacturer—whose three-year terms begin January 1, 2027. Grants the board rulemaking, licensing, investigatory, and enforcement authority, including hiring a hearing officer and employing investigators. Civil penalties (up to $1,000 per violation) may be imposed by the board and must be remitted to the State Treasurer for constitutionally prescribed distribution. Amends definitions in the Uniform Standard Code for Manufactured Homes and Recreational Vehicles to recognize dealers licensed under the new act and retains prior seals issued by the Department of Health and Human Services Regulation and Licensure or the Public Service Commission. Operative date: October 1, 2026. No direct appropriations or new funding streams are specified. Creates a state regulatory board to administer the new Recreational Vehicle Industry Regulation Act with authority to license dealers, manufacturers, and distributors; adopt and enforce rules; employ a hearing officer; and use investigators to inspect licensees. The board’s seal will authenticate records; the chair must review board actions if a controlling number of members are active market participants. Governor must appoint one dealer and one manufacturer board member by Jan. 1, 2027, each for three-year terms starting Jan. 1, 2027. Civil penalties (up to $1,000 per violation) are payable to the State Treasurer for distribution under Article VII, §5 of the Nebraska Constitution. Actions and appeals use county courts and the Administrative Procedure Act. The bill references existing statutes (Motor Vehicle Registration Act; Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act) but contains no new appropriations or budget line-item funding. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1122_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1122_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Health and Human Services LB1122 expresses legislative intent regarding the Department of Health and Human Services’ FY2026-27 appropriation for Medicaid nursing facility rates (Program No. 348) set at $462,480,546 (breakdown between General and Federal funds not specified). The bill directs that this total be used in the Program No. 348 rate calculation, including the annual inflation factor, and includes amounts for rate enhancement and other Medicaid nursing facility purposes. It requires DHHS to file: (1) an electronic report by August 1, 2026, explaining how the FY2026-27 inflation factor was calculated; and (2) an electronic report between December 15–31, 2026, identifying any remaining unobligated prior appropriations, encumbrances, and retroactive payments. The act takes effect immediately as an emergency measure. For DHHS: the bill states the Legislature’s intent that Program No. 348 receive a total Medicaid nursing facility rates appropriation of $462,480,546 for FY2026‑27 (General/Federal split not specified) and requires that this total be used in the Program No. 348 rate calculation, including the annual inflation factor. The total is to cover rate enhancements and other Medicaid nursing facility purposes. DHHS must file (1) an August 1, 2026 report to the Legislative Fiscal Analyst and Clerk explaining how the FY2026‑27 inflation factor was calculated, and (2) a Dec 15–31, 2026 report identifying any remaining unobligated prior appropriations, including encumbrances and retroactive payments. 109-2-LB1123_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1123_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Correctional Services LB1123 explicitly includes the Department of Correctional Services in its definitions and coverage. Correctional officers employed by the Department are treated as "officers" and the Department is listed as a "public safety agency," making its employees subject to the bill's Brady‑Giglio procedures (notice, reconsideration, and judicial review), confidentiality protections (redaction of personal information and limits on public release of photographs), and anti‑retaliation provisions. The bill imposes duties on prosecuting and public safety agencies that therefore apply to the Department. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department of Correctional Services are included. Key additions affecting the Department of Correctional Services (DCS):\n\n- Defines "officer" to include correctional officers employed by DCS and names DCS as a "public safety agency." \n- Bars discharge, discipline, certificate suspension/revocation solely because a prosecuting agency placed an officer on a Brady‑Giglio list. \n- Requires notice and allows officers ten business days to request reconsideration (or until Feb 1, 2028 if no notice received). Prosecutors may later remove names; duty to disclose Brady‑Giglio material remains. \n- Provides district court review (in camera, sealed) of denied reconsideration requests with limited standards for reversal. \n- Restricts public release of officer photos and mandates redaction of personal information; permits release to counsel/representatives. \n- Prohibits retaliation for exercising these rights.\n\nNo funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for DCS are included. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1124_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1124_Intro_Copy.docx LB1124 reallocates cigarette-tax proceeds and directs specific distributions beginning July 1, 2026. It retains the Tax Commissioner’s role in collection and assigns the State Treasurer responsibility for distributions. Key allocations: an amount equivalent to $0.52 per pack to the General Fund; an amount equivalent to $0.97 per pack plus an additional $1,250,000 annually to the Nebraska Health Care Cash Fund (the $0.97 equivalent earmarked for Medicaid); $3,820,000 annually to the Nebraska Public Safety Communication System Cash Fund; prior allocations to the Nebraska Outdoor Recreation Development Cash Fund, the Health and Human Services Cash Fund, and the Building Renewal Allocation Fund remain; any remaining proceeds go to the Nebraska Capital Construction Fund. Operative July 1, 2026, with an emergency clause making the act effective on enactment. Adds legislative findings that Nebraska spends over $120 million annually on Medicaid costs from smoking-related illness, that such illnesses are preventable, and that Medicaid consumes over 20% of the State General Fund. Directs that a portion of cigarette tax revenue be dedicated to Medicaid—specifically, an amount equivalent to $0.97 of the cigarette tax will be used for Medicaid purposes, effective July 1, 2026. Agencies affected: the Legislature (policy direction) and the State Medicaid program (recipient of the dedicated tax revenue). DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1125_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1125_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Administrative Services LB1125 amends §85‑422 to require that any University of Nebraska Facilities Program balance in excess of amounts needed for debt service (excluding amounts in the trust fund under §85‑421(7)) be distributed proportionally between the Board of Regents and the Department of Administrative Services. The split is based on the total amounts contributed to the program by the Board (per §85‑419) and by the state. The distribution period begins with the fiscal year commencing July 1, 2009, and continues through the fiscal year ending June 30, 2062, until December 31, 2063, or until all related financing obligations are discharged, whichever occurs first. Department of Administrative Services: No provisions in the added text affect the Department of Administrative Services, nor do they change any appropriations, funding, or budget allocations.\n\nSummary of added provisions:\n- University of Nebraska contracts to acquire a controlling or sole interest in any hospital or health care facility valued over $100 million require prior approval by the Legislature, or by the Legislative Council Executive Board if the Legislature is not in session.\n- A hospital or academic health center that is the primary affiliate of UNMC colleges cannot be owned or controlled (directly or indirectly) by a for‑profit or out‑of‑state entity unless the Attorney General, in consultation with the Board of Regents, determines such ownership/control is in the public interest. 109-2-LB1126_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1126_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Motor Vehicles, Department of Transportation LB1126 assigns significant roles and funding authority to the Department of Transportation (DOT) and updates Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) duties:\n\n- Infrastructure Development Investment Program: a commission-administered fund (with DOT administrative accounts) may receive appropriations, federal/state/local money, bond proceeds, etc.; intent that funds be appropriated each fiscal year for program purposes. The investment program makes loans via the department; repayments, earnings, and debt‑service remittances are credited to the fund. If a borrower defaults, the program may seek legislative re‑appropriation from the borrower's appropriations.\n\n- Transportation Innovation Act/unsolicited proposals: DOT may charge/retain up to $500 for evaluations, spend money appropriated to it to review/implement unsolicited proposals, enter contracts, and must report P3 activity annually to legislative committees.\n\n- Accident reporting/licensing/security: peace officers must report accidents to DOT; DOT classifies reports and electronically forwards Part II to DMV. DMV may suspend operator licenses after DOT receipt; minimum security under the Motor Vehicle Safety Responsibility Act set at $2,000.\n\n- Permits: DOT permit fees adjusted—general permit cap $50; continuous permits tiered ($50/90‑day; $100/180‑day; $200/year); certain 30‑day permits cap $50 (renewable); superload single‑trip fees set ($250/$400/$800) plus direct cost recovery; building‑move permit cap $50. Department of Transportation (DOT)\n- Creates the Infrastructure Development Investment Program Fund, administered by a commission. Fund sources: legislative transfers, federal/state/local grants, donations, repayments, bond proceeds, etc. Repayments and investment earnings are credited to the fund; debt service remitted to the State Treasurer is credited to the fund. Investment and accounting must follow state law, GAAP, annual independent audit. Legislature intends the fund be appropriated each fiscal year for program purposes.\n- Fund may be used for loans/financial assistance to eligible entities, reserves/credit enhancements, administrative costs (including DOT portfolio monitoring/collection), refinancing, and pooled financings. Account structure includes federal, state/local, and administrative accounts; administrative accounts are for DOT program administration.\n- Political subdivisions may apply to DOT for loans; on default DOT can pursue remedies, draw on reserves/credit facilities, or request the Legislature reduce a borrower’s appropriation and transfer funds to repay debt.\n- DOT may charge and retain up to $500 for initial evaluation/review of unsolicited project proposals, spend appropriated funds to review/develop/implement such proposals, and enter contracts for proposals.\n\nDepartment of Motor Vehicles (DMV)\n- No substantive changes or funding/appropriation provisions affecting the DMV in the added text.\n\nFees\n- Caps single-trip superload permit fees at $250 (≤300,000 lbs), $400 (>300,000–≤500,000 lbs), and $800 (>500,000 lbs); DOT may also recover direct permit-issuance costs. 109-2-LB1127_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1127_Intro_Copy.docx LB1127 amends Nebraska Game Law to authorize and regulate new "hangtag" permits and to revise permit display and procurement rules. The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission (the commission) is directed to set permit types and fees: resident annual permits up to $50, nonresident at twice that amount; temporary permits up to $10 (nonresident double); hangtag permits priced as the sum of one resident annual permit, one duplicate annual permit, plus a convenience fee (convenience fee capped at $15); active‑duty military permits $5. Disabled‑veteran permits are issued by the commission without charge based on U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs determinations. Permits may be sold via central and district commission offices and designated state park areas; county offices and commission‑designated private agents may continue to issue permits and retain issuing fees under section 37‑406. The commission may adopt implementing rules.\n\n[NOTE: Budget-related content may be missing from this summary. Please review manually.] Adds a new hangtag permit, effective Jan 1, 2027. The permit fee equals the cost of one resident annual permit plus one duplicate annual permit plus a commission-established convenience fee (capped at $15). The hangtag is valid through Dec. 31 of the issuance year, is vehicle-specific but may be moved between vehicles registered to the same Nebraska resident, and may not be reproduced or replaced if lost or stolen. Display rules require hanging from the rearview mirror or placement on the front dash if no mirror. Hangtags may be obtained from the commission’s central and district offices and at designated Nebraska state park system locations. No explicit appropriations or budget allocations are added. 109-2-LB1128_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1128_Intro_Copy.docx LB1128 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §53-123.17 to allow local governing bodies (city/village) to designate entertainment districts with designated consumption-only areas and to file that designation with the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. It creates a new consumption-only class entertainment district license for businesses lacking retail/craft brewery/microdistillery/manufacturer licenses. Consumption-only applications require commission approval and a $25 fee payable to the commission; existing eligible licensees pay a $300 additional entertainment-district fee payable to the local clerk. The commission must notify the clerk when applications are filed and process applications per §53-132. Local governing bodies may revoke designations, cancel licenses for cause, regulate by ordinance, and impose an occupation tax under §53-132. Appeals go to the commission under §53-134. No state appropriations or other budgetary allocations are added. Creates a new "consumption-only" class of entertainment district license. Local governing bodies must designate consumption-only areas and preapprove applicants. The Nebraska Liquor Control Commission (referred to as "the commission") will accept applications on commission-prescribed forms and issue the license if local approval exists; a $25 application fee is payable to the commission. The license lets a business (which does not sell or serve alcohol and lacks other liquor licenses) permit patrons to carry alcoholic beverages purchased from other entertainment district licensees into and out of its premises, subject to the Nebraska Liquor Control Act (including prohibitions on underage consumption). No other appropriations or budgetary changes are added. DOCX | PDF
109-2-LB1129_Intro Referral Legislature 109, Session 2 (2026) 109 2 LB1129_Intro_Copy.docx Department of Economic Development, Department of Labor, Department of Revenue - Department of Economic Development: required to (1) develop the standard form redevelopers must use for expedited-review redevelopment plans and (2) annually update workforce housing construction-cost caps using the Producer Price Index (PPI).\n\n- Department of Revenue: required to develop a standard certification form for county assessors to certify completion of improvements and valuation increases for expedited-review projects.\n\n- Department of Labor: the bill cites the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics PPI as the data source for the annual cost updates.\n\nNo new appropriations, funding transfers, or budget allocations to these agencies are specified in the bill. Added language expands eligibility to include underdeveloped parcels that have been within a city's extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction for more than 25 years and clarifies that a local governing body may designate an area as substandard/blighted if it shows higher-than-average unemployment and poverty using any local data when federal data is unreliable. It also expressly authorizes carrying out development of such underdeveloped extraterritorial parcels. The amendment does not reference the Department of Economic Development, Department of Labor, or Department of Revenue, nor does it include any changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.
